title: Do Not Blame Me, You Two: What I Bear Is Blame Enough
intro: Abd Yaghuth ibn Waqqas al-Harithi, chief of Banu al-Harith ibn Ka'b and leader of Madhhij at the Second Day of al-Kulab, made this poem after his side was routed and he was taken by Taym al-Ribab, who would accept nothing but his death in return for their own chief, al-Nu'man ibn Jassas, killed that day; it is the thirtieth poem of al-Mufaddaliyyat. The sources tell the rest differently: Abu Ubayda in the Naqa'id and Abu al-Faraj in al-Aghani say his captors tied his tongue with a leather strap so that he could not satirise them; al-Anbari reports both that they gagged him until he swore not to lampoon them and that the strap is only a figure of speech; al-Aghani says he asked for a noble death and they gave him wine and cut the great vein of his forearm, while Ibn Habib says he was beheaded. The poem tells two companions to stop blaming him, sends a rider with his farewell to his drinking friends in Najran, curses his tribe for running, tells of the strap and the old woman who laughed at him, and ends in pride at his generosity and horsemanship and grief for what he will never do again. Al-Jahiz wrote that “nothing on earth is more astonishing than Tarafa ibn al-Abd and Abd Yaghuth”, since the verses they made with death around them were no worse than those they made in safety.

translation: Do not blame me, you two: what I bear is blame enough;
blaming does no good to you, and none to me.
1.sharh: He asks his two companions to stop reproaching him: captivity and the death he is waiting for are reproach enough, and blame helps no one. In the story two men are left to taunt him, so al-Baghdadi takes the two as real people.

translation: Do you not know that reproach
does little good? And it is not my way to blame a brother.
2.sharh: Blame changes nothing, and he himself has never been one to blame his brother, so he should not be blamed now. He answers their reproach by pointing to his own character.

translation: O rider, if you reach al-Arud, tell
my drinking friends in Najran that we will never meet again.
3.sharh: He calls on any rider at all, not a particular one, to carry his farewell to his drinking friends in Najran: they will never meet again, because he is about to be killed. Sibawayh cites the line for calling out to no one in particular.

translation: Abu Karib, and the two Ayhams both,
and Qays of Yemen, in the uplands of Hadramawt.
4.sharh: He names the friends who should hear the news, the men he used to drink with, remembering them at the point of death. Al-Baghdadi reports that when the line reached Qays he said, “At your call, even though you put me last.”

translation: May God repay my people for al-Kulab with shame,
the pure of blood among them and the allies too.
5.sharh: He curses his own tribe for fleeing at al-Kulab and leaving him behind, both those of pure descent and the allies who fought with them. Abu Ubayda's version begins “God damn the horsemen I called on at al-Kulab”.

translation: Had I wished, a tall mare would have carried me clear of the horses,
and you would have seen the best dark steeds trailing behind her.
6.sharh: He could have escaped: his mare was fast enough to leave even the finest horses behind. Al-Asma'i explains that he names the dark horses tinged with green because they were thought the hardiest and the lightest of bone when lathered from running.

translation: But I stood guarding the honour of your fathers,
and the spears snatch away the one who stands his ground.
7.sharh: Turning to his tribe, he says he was taken because he stayed to defend what they were bound to defend, while they ran. Spears carry off the man who stands firm, so his capture proves his courage, not his weakness.

translation: I said, when they had bound my tongue with a strap:
“Men of Taym, set my tongue free.”
8.sharh: He recalls begging his captors to loosen his tongue. In al-Anbari's account they gagged him with a strap for fear of his satire, and freed him once he swore to blame only his own people and mourn himself; in another, the strap is a figure: only kindness will loosen his tongue.

translation: Men of Taym, you have me in your power, so be lenient:
your brother's blood is not mine to pay.
9.sharh: He asks them to be generous now that they hold him. He did not kill their chief, al-Anbari explains, so he is not the one whose death should pay for him. Ahmad, quoted in the same commentary, reads it as a boast: the dead man was not his equal.

translation: If you kill me, you kill a lord in me,
and if you let me go, you strip me of all I own.
10.sharh: Killing him means killing a chief; sparing him means taking his whole fortune as ransom. He offers everything he has and reminds them of his worth at the same time. Ibn Rashiq called the line “great spirit and toughness”.

translation: Is it true, O servants of God, that I will never hear
the herdsmen calling as they drive the camels far to pasture?
11.sharh: He grieves that he will never again hear the herdsmen singing out as they take their camels, some with newborn calves and some still due, to distant grazing. A sound of daily desert life becomes what he loses for ever.

translation: An old woman of Abd Shams laughs at me,
as though she had never seen a captive from Yemen before.
12.sharh: An old woman of the clan that caught him laughs at him. Al-Aghani says she was his young captor's mother: seeing so big and handsome a man, she asked who he was, and when he said “The chief of the people”, she laughed at a chief taken by such a fool.

translation: The women of the tribe stayed standing around me,
wanting from me what my own women want.
13.sharh: The women of the camp crowd round him and will not leave, wanting from him what his wives want. The commentators are silent; the likelier reading is a boast that even as a prisoner he draws women's eyes. The line is missing from al-Aghani and al-Iqd.

translation: My wife Mulayka knows well
that I am the lion, whether set upon or setting upon others.
14.sharh: His wife knows him as a lion both when he is attacked and when he attacks. He calls on the one who knows him best to say that captivity has not changed what he is.

translation: I used to slaughter camels for feasting and drive
the riding camels hard, and go where no living man would go.
15.sharh: He slaughtered camels to feed people, wore out his mounts on long journeys, and went where everyone else was afraid to go. Generosity and daring come together, as the list of what he has lost begins.

translation: I would slaughter my own mount for noble drinking companions,
and tear my cloak in two between the singing girls.
16.sharh: He would kill the camel he rode to feed his fellow drinkers, and split his cloak so that each of two singing girls had half. His generosity reached even the things he could not do without.

translation: When the spears made the horses shy and bolt,
my fingers were deft at turning the lance.
17.sharh: When horses panicked under the spears, he handled his lance with skill. Al-Marzuqi quotes this half for the expert who works his spear with his fingertips rather than gripping it in his whole fist.

translation: Many a charging band, spreading like locusts, I held back
with my hand, when they had turned their spear points on me.
18.sharh: He held off whole raiding parties, as many as a swarm of locusts, with his own hand, even when every spear point was aimed at him. Al-Anbari takes the charging band as men, others as horses.

translation: As though I had never ridden a thoroughbred, nor cried
to my horsemen, “Charge again! Give my men on foot some room!”
19.sharh: All that is gone now, as if he had never ridden a fine horse or ordered his cavalry to charge again and relieve his infantry. This line and the next follow Imru' al-Qays: “As though I had never ridden a horse for pleasure”.

translation: Nor bought the brimming wineskin, nor said
to true companions at the gaming arrows, “Make my fire blaze high!”
20.sharh: As if he had never bought a full skin of wine for his friends, or told his gaming companions to build up his fire. The commentators are silent on the fire; the likelier reading is the hospitality fire, raised high so night travellers would see it and come.

1.1.7.meaning: Biya: bi, “with me”, its final vowel lengthened for the rhyme, as at the end of every line.

3.1.4.head: عَرَضَ
3.1.4.meaning: You come to al-Arud: Mecca, Medina and the country around them; some add Yemen.

3.2.3.meaning: Najran: a town on the Hijaz side of Yemen.

4.1.1-2.meaning: Abu Karib: Bishr ibn Alqama ibn al-Harith, according to Ibn al-Athir.

4.1.3.head: الأَيهَمان
4.1.3.meaning: The two Ayhams: al-Aswad ibn Alqama ibn al-Harith and al-Aqib Abd al-Masih ibn al-Abyad, according to Ibn al-Athir.

4.2.1.head: قَيس
4.2.1.meaning: Qays ibn Ma'dikarib of Kinda, father of al-Ash'ath ibn Qays.

4.2.3.meaning: Hadramawt: a wide region east of Aden, near the sea.

5.1.4.head: الكُلاب
5.1.4.meaning: Al-Kulab: a watering place seven nights from al-Yamama, where two famous battles were fought; this is the second.

5.2.3.head: المَوالي
5.2.3.meaning: Mawali: here, allies who joined the tribe without sharing its descent.

6.2.3.head: الحُوّ
6.2.3.meaning: Huww: horses of a dark colour shading into green.

7.1.3.head: ذِمار
7.1.3.meaning: Dhimar: what a man is bound to protect, such as his protégé and his right to vengeance.

8.1.5.head: نِسعَة
8.1.5.meaning: Nis'a: a plaited leather strap, of the kind used to tie on a camel's saddle.

8.2.1-2.meaning: Taym: Taym al-Ribab, the tribe of al-Nu'man ibn Jassas, who held him captive.

9.2.6.head: بَواء
9.2.6.meaning: Bawa': an equal in blood, a man whose killing is fair requital for another's.

11.2.4.head: المَتالي
11.2.4.meaning: Matali: a herd of she-camels some of which have calved while the rest have not.

12.1.4.head: عَبشَمِيّ
12.1.4.meaning: Of Abd Shams, a clan of Sa'd ibn Zayd Manat of Tamim.

12.2.3.head: رَأى
12.2.3.meaning: Seen. Keeping the long vowel after lam is irregular: al-Farra' derives it from tar'a with its hamza softened, and al-Akhfash held the right reading to be taray, “you had seen”, addressed to her.

15.1.6.meaning: The article of al-matiyy, “the riding camels”, which runs over into the second half.

16.2.3.head: القَينَة
16.2.3.meaning: Qayna: a slave woman, here a singing girl.

18.1.1.head: عادِيَة
18.1.1.meaning: Adiya: a band charging in a raid; some take it as charging horses.

19.2.5.head: رِجال
19.2.5.meaning: Rijal: here men fighting on foot.

20.1.2.head: سَبَأَ
20.1.2.meaning: Buy wine, to drink rather than to sell.

20.2.1.head: أَيسار
20.2.1.meaning: Aysar: players of maysir, the gambling game with arrows.
